alignment.note: The Vulgate omits Peter's entire speech (Greek καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς ... μίαν), replacing it with an editorial comment explaining Peter's confusion (Non enim sciebat quid diceret: erant enim timore exterriti). This represents a substantive redactional divergence where the Latin tradition substitutes narrative commentary for direct discourse.

Greek uses the article + proper name construction (ὁ Πέτρος); Peshitta employs the bare proper name ܟܐܦܐ (Kepha, the Aramaic equivalent). The Vulgate omits Peter as subject entirely, having replaced his speech with third-person narration.

Greek λέγει τῷ Ἰησοῦ employs a present-tense verb with dative indirect object; Peshitta uses ܠܗ (to him) as pronominal suffix, avoiding the proper name. The Vulgate replaces this entire clause with quid diceret (what he might say), shifting from direct to indirect discourse.
Both Greek ῥαββί and Peshitta ܪܒܝ preserve the vocative address to Jesus; the Vulgate omits this entirely as part of its replacement of Peter's speech with editorial commentary.

Greek καλόν ἐστιν ἡμᾶς ὧδε εἶναι uses an impersonal construction with accusative + infinitive; Peshitta ܫܦܝܪ ܗܘ ܠܢ ܕܗܪܟܐ ܢܗܘܐ employs a predicate adjective with dative pronoun and ܕ-clause. The Vulgate omits Peter's proposal entirely, substituting Non enim sciebat quid diceret to explain his confusion.

Greek καὶ ποιήσωμεν τρεῖς σκηνάς uses a hortatory subjunctive (let us make); Peshitta ܘܢܥܒܕ ܬܠܬ ܡܛܠܝܢ employs a cohortative imperfect. The Vulgate omits this proposal, replacing it with erant enim timore exterriti (for they were terrified with fear), an explanatory gloss not present in Greek or Syriac.

Greek σοὶ μίαν (for you one) and Peshitta ܠܟ ܚܕܐ are semantically aligned, using dative pronoun + cardinal numeral. The Vulgate omits the entire tabernacle distribution as part of its redactional replacement of Peter's speech.

Greek καὶ Μωϋσεῖ μίαν and Peshitta ܘܠܡܘܫܐ ܚܕܐ both allocate one tabernacle to Moses using conjunction + dative proper name + numeral. The Vulgate's omission continues its substitution of Peter's direct speech with narrative commentary.

Greek καὶ Ἠλίᾳ μίαν and Peshitta ܘܠܐܠܝܐ ܚܕܐ complete the triadic distribution with identical syntax. The Vulgate omits this, concluding instead with its editorial explanation of Peter's fear-induced confusion.

The Vulgate adds an entirely unique clause (Non enim sciebat quid diceret: erant enim timore exterriti) not present in Greek or Peshitta, providing third-person narrative commentary on Peter's mental state rather than his actual words. This represents a major redactional divergence, possibly harmonizing with Mark 9:6 or reflecting Latin exegetical tradition that emphasizes the disciples' fear over Peter's proposal.
